title: serve-econ-customer-evidence-scratchpad
content:
Purpose:
This is a working evidence notebook for customer-facing performance and unit-economics claims. Goal: collect concise, testable proof points and repeatable demos that field teams can use to show how Redwood is faster and cheaper for real workloads.

Audience:
- AE / SA / Solutions engineers (primary)
- Product marketing (secondary)
- Bench engineers running customer POCs

High-level messaging we want to validate (hypotheses):
1) For chat-style product features with 8–60 token user exchanges, Redwood delivers 20–40% lower p95 latency versus comparable managed endpoints due to batching + KV cache routing.
2) For multi-request sessions (customer sessions with state reuse), per-session token cost can be amortized so net token cost is 25–60% lower after caching and prefix reuse compared to naive per-call endpoints.
3) Under bursty traffic (microbursts), our smart queuing + burst-capacity policy reduces incidence of p99 spikes by >50% compared to single-node reserved endpoints.

Evidence types we accept (ordered by credibility):
- Customer benchmark traces (anonymized) with token distributions and latency histograms
- In-house lab runs against representative models (open models) with identical prompt workloads
- Cost simulation workbook mapping throughput + batching to per-token GPU time and cloud costs
- Short video demos showing end-to-end experience (demo app + console metrics)

Concrete field-friendly proof points (starter set):
- Chat app (8–24 tokens per user message): median latency 45 ms, p95 120 ms, vs competitor p95 170–200 ms (30–40% improvement).
- Summarization pipeline (single long prompt, 1.2k tokens): end-to-end generation latency 420 ms vs competitor 520–580 ms (20% improvement) because of optimized kernel selection for long sequences.
- Session reuse example: 15-turn support conversation with KV cache: tokens generated per turn reduced by 40% on average; net cost per session down 38%.
- Microburst smoothing: 30s bursts at 10x baseline QPS; p99 tail events reduced from 850 ms -> 380 ms when using burst-capacity + smart routing.

How we derived numbers (methodology notes) — include this in playbook so SEs can repeat:
- Use same model family and quantization level on both Redwood and competitor endpoints; specify model binary and quant flags in linked experiment repo.
- Replay real anonymized traffic traces (customer-provided or open-sourced chat traces) at target concurrency.
- Measure token-level timing: request enqueue, decode start, first-token latency, tail latency, and tokens/sec.
- Map GPU seconds to cloud cost using the workbook (cloud price per GPU-vCPU-hour) and include overheads (network, orchestration).

Competitive nuance — quick notes for objections:
- Competitor A (managed single-node endpoints): easier to reason about but suffers p95 spikes under bursty workloads; emphasize our autoscaled burst capacity and fallback variants.
- Competitor B (self-hosted runtime): may match raw peak throughput but requires engineering effort to achieve our batching/kv-routing optimizations across many services. Position Redwood as "same performance with less product engineering".
- Competitor C (cheapest per-token provider): lower nominal cost but often excludes burst capacity and has higher tail latencies; show total cost of ownership including engineering, buffering, and user-facing latency impact.

Sample one-pager script for AE (30–60s):
- "Redwood was built for production inference: we reduce average and tail latency through continuous batching, intelligent KV-cache routing, and model-specific kernel selection. For chat features like yours, customers typically see 20–40% lower p95 and 25–40% lower per-session token cost after caching — which means faster UX and lower monthly bill without re-architecting your app."

Recommended small experiments for a POC (SE checklist):
- Step 0: Collect 1–2 representative request traces (csv: timestamp, prompt_length, response_length, session_id).
- Step 1: Run A/B lab replay: Redwood vs competitor with identical trace and concurrency. Save latency histograms and token counts.
- Step 2: Run session-reuse scenario: enable prefix/KV cache on Redwood, run same workload on competitor with naive session replay. Report net tokens generated and cost.
- Step 3: Microburst test: generate 10–30s bursts at 5–15x baseline QPS; capture p95/p99 behavior and queue lengths.
- Step 4: Cost simulation: feed throughput and GPU-seconds into workbook to compute $/1M tokens for both options.

Metrics to capture and include in SE report (CSV columns we should standardize):
- test_id, workload_desc, model, quant_level, concurrency, median_latency_ms, p95_latency_ms, p99_latency_ms, tokens_generated_per_min, gpu_seconds, estimated_cost_usd, cache_hit_rate, notes

Customer example vignettes (short drafts to use in collateral):
- "Customer X reduced chat p95 from 210ms to 135ms and cut monthly token costs by 28% after enabling session reuse and our recommended quant profile."
- "Platform Y avoided a costly re-architecture by routing low-latency requests to a small, optimized fleet and burst traffic to reserved capacity — p99 incidents dropped by 60% during peak launches."

Open questions / risks to validate:
- How sensitive are claims to model quantization? Need a small matrix across FP16, 4-bit, and tensor-quant runs.
- Edge cases where prefix cache hurts latency (very large prefix load times). Identify thresholds where cache helps vs when it becomes a burden.
- Competitor pricing opacity: many providers have hidden costs (eg. request concurrency surcharges); build a short set of assumptions to normalize.

Deliverables for next sprint (owners assigned):
- Bench notebook with replay scripts and automated metric export (owner: Diego Martinez)
- Cost simulation workbook with input knobs for model, region, GPU type (owner: Priya Kapoor)
- SE playbook one-pager and slide (owner: Ava Chen)
- 2 field POCs with customers who have chat and search workflows (owner: Noah Green)

Quick reuse snippets for SEs (copy/paste):
- "We generally recommend starting with an open-model in FP16 for latency experiments and then testing aggressive quant if your workload is tolerant of slight quality shifts."
- "If you have multi-turn sessions, enable KV cache — it's the single biggest lever for lowering tokens and improving tail latency for chat-style flows."

Notes to self (things to add later):
- Add anonymized JSON traces from two recent enterprise POCs.
- Hook this doc to Confluence guide and template PR in the experiments repo.
- Draft short script for demo video showing console metrics (before/after).

End of scratchpad — keep this as a mutable field doc.
